nj_charity_care.applies_to: all NJ acute care hospitals, hospital care only (not physician/anesthesia/radiology reading/outpatient Rx)

wa_charity_care.applies_to: every WA hospital licensed under RCW 70.41.020(9), per RCW 70.170.020's definition -- includes Critical Access Hospitals (no exclusion in the licensing definition); patient responsibility portion of hospital charges
wa_charity_care.note: RCW 70.170.060(5) sets TWO schedules: a more generous one for larger hospital systems/hospitals (defined by owning 3+ acute hospitals, or specific large hospitals in King County or a southern-border county), and this floor schedule required of every other hospital. CareMap doesn't have hospital bed-count/ownership-network data loaded to tell which hospitals qualify for the larger-system schedule, so this is the legal MINIMUM every WA hospital must offer -- some hospitals are required to offer better terms (up to 400% FPL). Confirm with the specific hospital.

eligibility.must_be_un_or_underinsured: unconfirmed -- the statute's income-based eligibility doesn't explicitly require uninsured status the way NJ's does; applied conservatively here (same uninsured-only gate as NJ) pending fuller verification
eligibility.not_medicaid_eligible: unconfirmed -- hospitals must help Medicaid-eligible patients apply for Medicaid first, but the statute doesn't flatly exclude them from charity care the way NJ's does

il_charity_care.source: https://codes.findlaw.com/il/chapter-210-health-facilities-and-regulation/il-st-sect-210-89-10/ (210 ILCS 89/10 and 89/5, Hospital Uninsured Patient Discount Act)
il_charity_care.applies_to: all IL hospitals -- uninsured patients only (the statute does not mention underinsured patients at all, unlike NJ/WA)
il_charity_care.note: Verified directly against the current codified text (210 ILCS 89/5 and /10). Below the free-care threshold, patient_pays_pct is a real, exact 0% -- no gap there. ABOVE it, the law does NOT set a clean percentage: the discount is charges x (1 - cost_to_charge_ratio x 1.35), a real statutory formula, but it needs each hospital's own Medicare cost-to-charge ratio, which CareMap doesn't have loaded (it's a different CMS dataset -- cost reports -- not the Hospital General Information / DRG charge data already in use). A hard cap also applies there: a hospital can never collect more than 20% of the patient's family income in any 12-month period, regardless of the formula result. CareMap deliberately shows NO percentage above the free-care threshold rather than guess one -- only the free-care floor and the 20%-income-cap fact are real without that missing data.

ny_charity_care.source: https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/PBH/2807-K (NY Public Health Law 2807-k(9) and (9-a), Hospital Financial Assistance Law, amended 2024-04-20)
ny_charity_care.applies_to: all NY general hospitals -- uninsured AND underinsured patients (unlike IL, which is uninsured-only)
ny_charity_care.note: Verified directly against the current codified text (PBH 2807-k(9-a), post-2024-04-20 amendment -- an older DOH advisory letter citing a 300% FPL ceiling is stale; the current ceiling is 400%). Below the free-care threshold, patient_pays_pct is a real, exact 0% -- 'no nominal payment shall be collected' per the statute itself. ABOVE it, the law does NOT discount a percentage of billed charges the way NJ/WA/IL do: it caps payment at 10% (201-300% FPL) or 20% (301-400% FPL) of the MEDICAID-EQUIVALENT rate for the service, a completely different dollar base than the typical billed charge CareMap has from CMS Medicare Inpatient by Provider and Service. CareMap has no Medicaid-rate data loaded at all, so there isn't even a disclosable cap fact to surface above the threshold the way IL's 20%-of-income cap is (that one needs no extra dataset; NY's does). CareMap deliberately shows NO percentage and NO cap fact above the free-care threshold -- only the free-care floor is real without Medicaid-rate data. Above 400% FPL the statute is silent (hospital's own policy).

eligibility.not_medicaid_eligible: unconfirmed -- immigration/documentation status is explicitly barred as a criterion (9-a(a)), but the statute doesn't flatly exclude Medicaid-eligible patients the way NJ's does

or_charity_care.applies_to: Oregon NONPROFIT hospitals only (ORS 442.612(8): organized under ORS chapter 65 or IRC 501(c)) -- excludes for-profit and government-owned hospitals. CareMap gates this via CMS's own 'ownership' field (Voluntary non-profit - *): see charity_care_participant in build_data.py.
or_charity_care.note: Verified directly against the current codified text (ORS 442.610-442.618). Unlike IL/NY/CO, Oregon's dollar base is real billed charges (ORS 442.612(9): 'patient's cost' = charges billed net of insurance/public-program reimbursement) -- the exact CMS billed-charge figure CareMap already has, so the full sliding scale is computable, not just a free floor. These are statutory MINIMUM discounts (a hospital's own policy may be more generous, never less) -- same floor-schedule pattern as WA's RCW 70.170.060(5)(b), so patient_pays_pct here is the maximum a patient is guaranteed NOT to exceed, not a guessed exact figure. No uninsured/underinsured restriction found in the statute -- broader than every other state modeled (covers insured, underinsured, uninsured alike), but CareMap still only shows a charity-care price to the uninsured per the conservative gate applied everywhere else, since insured patients have a separate relevant number (their own cost-sharing) this app doesn't model.

eligibility.must_be_un_or_underinsured: not required by the statute itself (income-only test) -- applied conservatively here anyway, consistent with every other modeled state

md_charity_care.applies_to: every MD hospital under HSCRC (Health Services Cost Review Commission) jurisdiction -- virtually all MD acute care hospitals, regardless of ownership, under Maryland's unique all-payer rate-setting system
md_charity_care.note: Verified directly against the current codified text. One real wrinkle: the statute discounts the patient's 'out-of-pocket expense for the regulated hospital service', not 'charges' by name. For an INSURED patient that would mean something net of insurer payment -- but CareMap only ever shows a charity-care price to the UNINSURED (same conservative gate as every other state here), and for an uninsured patient there's no insurer payment to net against, so out-of-pocket expense collapses to the full regulated rate -- which, under Maryland's all-payer system, is the same rate CMS's own Medicare Inpatient by Provider and Service dataset reports for MD hospitals (unlike most states, Maryland's regulated rate and its Medicare-reported rate aren't materially different by design). This is an inference from the uninsured-only restriction, not a literal statutory statement that the base is 'billed charges' -- treated here the same honest way as WA's unconfirmed eligibility gate. Maryland also has a separate hardship tier (medical debt exceeding 25% of family income over 12 months, up to 500% FPL) that CareMap can't verify (needs the patient's actual debt history) and does not compute.

eligibility.asset_limit_note: may only count household monetary assets over $100,000 (19-214.1(b)(8)(i)), excluding certain retirement assets -- more generous than NJ's $7,500/$15,000

ri_charity_care.source: 216-RICR-40-10-23.14 (Rhode Island hospital licensing regulation, Provision of Charity Care, Uncompensated Care, and Community Benefits)
ri_charity_care.applies_to: every licensed RI hospital, as a condition of licensure (R.I. Gen. Laws 23-17-43) -- uninsured and underinsured patients alike
ri_charity_care.note: Verified directly against the current regulatory text. Section 23.14.1(A)(3) sets a real, exact 0% at or below 200% FPL -- no gap there. From 200-300% FPL, section 23.14.1(A)(6) requires a sliding scale but explicitly leaves the specific percentage at each band to EACH INDIVIDUAL HOSPITAL to set -- there is no statewide number to encode, not a missing-data problem like IL's cost-to-charge ratio, but an intentional delegation in the regulation itself. Above 300% FPL the regulation doesn't address pricing at all. Unlike IL (whose 20%-of-income cap is a disclosable fact even without a percentage), RI has no comparable fallback fact found -- CareMap shows NO percentage and NO cap fact above the free-care threshold, only the free-care floor is real here.

eligibility.asset_limit_note: optional per hospital (23.14.1(A)(4)) -- if used, $8,000 single / $12,000 family (2006 base, CPI-adjusted annually), primary residence and one vehicle excluded

ma_charity_care.source: 101 CMR 613.00, Health Safety Net (Mass. Gen. Laws c.118E) -- https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/massachusetts/101-CMR-613-04
ma_charity_care.applies_to: MA acute hospitals, reimbursed through the state Health Safety Net fund -- uninsured and underinsured patients alike
ma_charity_care.note: Verified directly against the current regulatory text. Below 150% FPL (613.04(6)(b)(3)), HSN 'Primary'/'Secondary' eligibility applies with no deductible -- a real, exact $0 out-of-pocket for HSN-covered services, though note this threshold is 150% FPL, LOWER than the 200% free-care line most other modeled states use. From 150-300% FPL ('Health Safety Net - Partial', 613.04(8)(c)(1)), the annual deductible is the GREATER of (a) the lowest-cost MA Health Connector premium for that household size, or (b) 40% x (200% FPL - household income) -- (b) alone is computable from income, but the deductible is legally the max of (a) and (b), and (a) needs Health Connector premium data CareMap doesn't have, so the true dollar amount isn't knowable here. It's also a flat annual deductible, not a percentage of billed charges, structurally unlike every other state modeled so far. Above 300% FPL, HSN's general categories don't apply at all -- only a separate Medical Hardship path requiring the patient's actual medical-expense history, which CareMap can't verify. CareMap shows NO percentage and NO cap fact above 150% FPL -- only the free-care floor is real here, closer to RI's 'no fact to add' framing than IL's disclosed cap.

eligibility.residency_requirement: unconfirmed -- secondary sources disagree on whether HSN requires MA residency; not independently confirmed against primary text, applied conservatively (same posture as WA's unconfirmed eligibility gate) pending fuller verification

me_charity_care.source: https://legislature.maine.gov/statutes/22/title22sec1716-A.html (22 M.R.S. 1716-A, enacted by PL 2025 c. 488, effective 2026-07-01; replaced the repealed 150% FPL rule in 22 M.R.S. 1716)
me_charity_care.applies_to: Maine hospitals (the statute doesn't define or limit 'hospital'; no ownership or type carve-out found) -- Maine residents only
me_charity_care.note: Verified against the current statute text: 1716-A(2) requires 'free, medically necessary services for patients whose family income ... is equal to or less than 200% of the federal poverty level.' There is no sliding scale above 200%, so CareMap shows no percentage there. One real fact still applies above the line and needs no extra data: 1716-A(8) requires hospitals to offer anyone with family income up to 400% FPL a payment plan whose monthly out-of-pocket payments do not exceed 4% of monthly family income. Eligibility is income-only in the statute (insured patients qualify too), but CareMap still only shows a charity-care price to the uninsured, as in every other state. Residency is required (1716-A(1)(F): living in Maine intending to stay, or having or seeking work there; tourists and visitors excluded) -- CareMap can't check this, so it's disclosed. No asset test (1716-A(4)(A)). Not confirmed verbatim: the 45-day decision window and 15-day missing-items notice were read through a summarizing fetch, so they're not encoded as fields. The 2026-07-01 effective date comes from the FindLaw mirror; the official page confirms 1716 was repealed and 1716-A is current.

eligibility.must_be_un_or_underinsured: not required by the statute (income-only) -- CareMap applies its uninsured-only display gate anyway

vt_charity_care.source: https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/section/18/221/09482 (18 V.S.A. 9481-9482, Act 119 of 2022, eff. 2022-07-01; secondary sources say hospital compliance was required by 2024-07-01)
vt_charity_care.applies_to: every hospital licensed under 18 V.S.A. chapter 43 (9481(6)), no size or ownership limit -- Vermont residents only (no minimum duration), plus people living in Vermont without stable housing
vt_charity_care.note: Verified against the current statute text. 9482(b)(2)(A): uninsured patients at or below 250% FPL get 'a 100 percent discount from the amount generally billed' -- a real $0, and 250% is the highest free-care line of any modeled state. From 250-400% FPL the law requires at least a 40% discount, but off the 'amount generally billed' (9481(1), the 501(r) look-back method), which is each hospital's own figure, not the CMS billed charge CareMap has -- so CareMap names that protection without a dollar figure. Up to 600% FPL, if the hospital's bills for a patient exceed 20% of household income, it must reduce the amount due to 20% of household income -- disclosable without extra data (the statute text gives no time period for this, so CareMap doesn't state one). Income is measured under the federal premium tax credit rules, so CareMap's percent-of-poverty figure is an approximation, as in other states. Not confirmed from primary text: that Critical Access Hospitals are covered (inferred, since chapter 43 licensing isn't limited by type) and the 2024 compliance date.

eligibility.must_be_un_or_underinsured: free-tier percentage applies to the uninsured; insured patients get out-of-pocket costs waived instead (9482(b)(2)(C)) -- CareMap shows charity-care prices to the uninsured only

nc_charity_care.source: https://www.ncdhhs.gov/medical-debt-toolkit/download?attachment (NCDHHS Medical Debt Initiative toolkit v1.1, 2026-10-12, Appendix 2 policy 2; participating hospitals: https://www.ncdhhs.gov/participating-hospitals-med-debt/open)
nc_charity_care.applies_to: the 99 hospitals participating in NC's Medical Debt Mitigation program (a condition of NC Medicaid's HASP enhanced hospital payments, effective 2025-01-01 and renewed each payment year -- not a state statute); NC residents only
nc_charity_care.note: Verified against the NCDHHS toolkit text (extracted directly from the PDF). Policy 2.b.i: 'Discount of 100% for individuals with incomes below 200% FPL' -- strictly below, so CareMap's free tier stops at 199% (with FPL rounded to a whole percent, a true 199.5-199.99% shows the gap message instead of $0, the conservative direction). 2.b.ii-iii: at least 75% off at 200-250% FPL and at least 50% at 250-300% FPL, but for the uninsured the base is 'the amount generally billed' (2.b.iv), a hospital-specific rate CareMap doesn't have, so no share is computed. 2.d: at 200-300% FPL the hospital must offer a payment plan of at most 36 months with monthly payments no greater than 5% of monthly household income. 2.c: emergency department visits may still be charged the greater of the discounted amount or $35 (not more than a health plan's cost-sharing). Participation was matched to CMS CCNs by name by hand against the official list (e.g. St. Luke's Hospital = AdventHealth Polk, renamed 2024); three CareMap NC hospitals aren't on it and are excluded in build_data.py.

eligibility.must_be_un_or_underinsured: not required (applies to insured and uninsured alike) -- CareMap shows charity-care prices to the uninsured only

nc_charity_care.free_tier_note: Emergency department visits may still be charged the greater of the discounted amount or $35. NC residents only.
nc_charity_care.gap_disclosure: NC has no computable percentage at or above 200% FPL -- say that plainly. Between 200% and 300% FPL, participating hospitals must give at least 75% (200-250%) or 50% (250-300%) off the hospital's own 'amount generally billed' -- a hospital-specific rate CareMap doesn't have, so give no dollar figure for it -- and must offer a payment plan of at most 36 months with monthly payments no greater than 5% of monthly household income. Above 300% FPL, none of that applies. NC residents only. This is a condition of NC's Medicaid hospital payment program that participating hospitals agreed to, not a state statute.

oh_charity_care.source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-5160-2-17 (OAC 5160-2-17, Hospital Care Assurance Program, eff. 2022-07-28; hospital scope ORC 5168.01, 5168.09)
oh_charity_care.applies_to: Ohio nonfederal general medical/surgical and pediatric general hospitals receiving Hospital Care Assurance Program payments (ORC 5168.01(F)), any ownership -- Ohio residents not receiving Medicaid
oh_charity_care.note: Verified against the current rule text. Paragraph (A): each hospital that receives payment under ORC Chapter 5168 must 'provide, without charge to the individual, basic, medically necessary hospital-level services' to Ohio residents 'whose income is at or below the federal poverty line' who aren't Medicaid recipients -- a real $0 at or below 100% FPL, the lowest free-care line of any modeled state. 'Basic, medically necessary' means inpatient and outpatient services Medicaid covers, excluding transplants. Nothing statewide above 100% FPL. Applications accepted until three years from the follow-up notice (not encoded as a field). Not confirmed: that every Chapter 5168 hospital actually receives an HCAP payment; most quotes came through a summarizing fetch with key phrases verbatim.

eligibility.must_be_un_or_underinsured: not required by the rule -- CareMap shows charity-care prices to the uninsured only

oh_charity_care.free_tier_note: Covers basic, medically necessary services (what Medicaid covers, excluding transplants). Ohio residents not on Medicaid.
oh_charity_care.gap_disclosure: OH has no statewide rule above its 100% FPL free-care line -- say that plainly and direct the user to that hospital's own financial assistance policy. Ohio's free care is for Ohio residents not on Medicaid.

sc_charity_care.source: https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t44c006.php (S.C. Code 44-6-150, last amended 2026 Act 146 eff. 2026-05-15) and https://www.scstatehouse.gov/coderegs/Chapter%20126.pdf (S.C. Code Regs. 126-500 to 126-560, Medically Indigent Assistance Program)
sc_charity_care.applies_to: SC general hospitals, for inpatient care of patients sponsored by the Medically Indigent Assistance Program -- eligibility is decided by the patient's county, not the hospital
sc_charity_care.note: Verified against the current statute and regulation text. Reg 126-520(C): only those 'equal to or less than one hundred percent of the poverty guidelines may qualify for full sponsorship'; 44-6-150(A) requires general hospitals to admit sponsored patients for inpatient care. Under Reg 126-535 a fully sponsored patient owes only liquid assets above $500, so $0 for covered inpatient care. 100-200% FPL is partial sponsorship whose share depends on a state 'mean MIAP payment amount' CareMap doesn't have, so it isn't computed. Conditions: other payment sources, including a Medicaid application if possibly eligible, must be exhausted first; SC residents who are US citizens or lawful permanent residents; liquid assets $500 or less, home equity up to $35,000, other property up to $6,000; inpatient Medicaid-covered services only, not physician fees. Not confirmed: what the 2026 amendment to 44-6-150(A)(2) changed (the current text was read, the diff wasn't), and the 2018 regulations describe hospital payments the statute says hospitals don't receive -- the patient's $0 follows from the regulation either way.

eligibility.must_be_un_or_underinsured: all other payment sources must be exhausted first

sc_charity_care.free_tier_note: Inpatient hospital care only, not physician bills, through South Carolina's Medically Indigent Assistance Program: the patient's county decides eligibility, liquid assets must be $500 or less, Medicaid and other coverage must be applied for first, and it's limited to SC residents who are US citizens or lawful permanent residents.
sc_charity_care.gap_disclosure: SC has no computable share above its 100% FPL line -- say that plainly. From 100-200% FPL the program offers partial sponsorship using a state payment figure CareMap doesn't have, so give no percentage or dollar figure. Eligibility is decided by the patient's county, not the hospital.

nv_charity_care.source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-439B.html (NRS 439B.260(1), last amended 2021; 'major hospital' defined in NRS 439B.115)
nv_charity_care.applies_to: Nevada 'major hospitals' only -- 200+ licensed or approved beds, or part of an affiliated in-county group with 200+ combined beds, and not government-operated -- for uninsured inpatients
nv_charity_care.note: Verified against the official statute text. NRS 439B.260(1): 'A major hospital shall reduce or discount the total billed charge by at least 30 percent for hospital services provided to an inpatient who' has no insurance, 'is not eligible for coverage by a state or federal program of public assistance', and 'makes reasonable arrangements within 30 days' of notice to pay. No income test, and the base is the total billed charge -- CareMap's own base -- so the patient pays at most 70% of it (a minimum discount, so an upper bound). Major hospitals were identified from CMS's Provider of Services bed counts and CMS hospital ownership data (affiliation = shared CMS-reported owner in the same county, since the statute doesn't define 'affiliated'); the CCN list is in build_data.py. University Medical Center (290007) is excluded as county-operated even though CMS labels it nonprofit. Carson Tahoe (290019, 211 total but 190 certified beds) is left out as not confirmed, since the statute counts state-licensed beds. CareMap can't check the public-assistance or 30-day conditions, so they're disclosed.
nv_charity_care.tier_note: Inpatient care only, at Nevada's major hospitals, if you aren't eligible for Medicaid or other public coverage (apply for that first if you might be) and you make reasonable payment arrangements within 30 days of the hospital's notice. It's a minimum discount, so you may owe less.

good_faith_estimate.applies_to: uninsured or self-pay patients scheduling care at least 3 business days ahead
